AvailableState and OccupiedState each expose a private constructor and a static getInstance() — every spot in the whole parking lot shares the SAME AvailableState object and the SAME OccupiedState object. Given neither state class holds a single field, why is sharing one instance across every spot completely safe?,It isn't fully safe — this is a bug the class hasn't caught yet,It's only safe because there happen to be very few spots in this specific parking lot,It's safe only because CompactSpot/LargeSpot/HeavySpot are declared final,"They're pure behavior objects — which spot is being acted on is passed in as a method argument (assign(this)/release(this)) rather than stored as a field on the state object, so there's nothing per-spot that a shared instance could ever get wrong",,4,"Stateless singletons are safe to share precisely because the varying piece (which spot) travels as a parameter, not as state on the object itself.",2

PricingStrategyFactory picks an IPricingStrategy per vehicle via getPricingStrategy(vehicle), instead of one calculateFee(ticket, size) method with an if-else chain living inside ParkingFacade.unPark(). What's the actual advantage of the Strategy version?,Strategy makes fee calculation run measurably faster at runtime,"Adding a new pricing rule (a genuinely different formula, not just a different rate) means writing one new class implementing IPricingStrategy — ParkingFacade.unPark() itself never has to be touched","There's no real advantage today since both existing strategies use the identical formula, just a different constant",Strategy is required here because Ticket is declared final,,2,New pricing rules become pure additions (a new class) instead of edits to unPark()'s own body — the same OCP payoff seen with Factory Method back in class-22.,2

HourlyBikePricingStrategy and HourlyCarPricingStrategy are identical except for one constant (15.0 vs 40.0). Given the earlier lesson that reflexively adding abstraction "just in case" is a premature-generalization risk, is keeping these as two separate classes still justified here?,"Yes — unlike a case where a whole new constructor parameter and interface get added for a variation that doesn't exist yet, the Strategy interface here already exists at zero extra structural cost, against a real likelihood that parking pricing rules diverge by vehicle type later",No — this is premature generalization and the two classes should be collapsed into one rate-parameterized class immediately,It's only justified because Java requires exactly one class per implements clause,There's no meaningful comparison to make between these two situations,,1,Cheap-to-keep abstraction against a plausible future need is a different tradeoff than adding real new complexity for a need that doesn't exist — that's the distinction that matters.,2

column2: assigning ""one"" of them occupies both, since they're really the same object, and capacity tracking breaks for any size with more than one spot",It throws a runtime exception since the same spot can't be added to a floor twice,"Two distinct objects, but they harmlessly share the same SpotSize enum reference",,2,"No `new` ever runs inside getSpot() — it only looks up an already-built instance from a static map, so every call for a given size returns the identical object.",3

column1: Setting the previous bug aside — why is calling this class SpotFactory misleading in GoF pattern terms specifically?,It isn't misleading at all — this is a textbook Factory Method implementation,It's misleading only because it uses a HashMap instead of a switch statement,It's misleading only because SpotSize is an enum rather than an int,"A real Factory is expected to construct a NEW object per call when the caller wants a new one
column2: this class instead looks up and returns a pre-built shared instance from a static map, with no new happening inside getSpot() at all — it behaves like a Registry/Flyweight, not a Factory",,4,"The naming mismatch is separate from the bug itself: this class was never doing construction, it was doing lookup.",2

column1: What's the minimal fix to make SpotFactory actually behave like a factory (return an independent object each call), while keeping the same method signature ISpot getSpot(SpotSize spotSize)?,Mark the existing CompactSpot/LargeSpot/HeavySpot instances as volatile,Change SpotSize from an enum to a class,"Replace Map<SpotSize, ISpot> with Map<SpotSize, Supplier<ISpot>> (or an equivalent per-size constructor reference), and call it inside getSpot() to produce a fresh instance each time, instead of storing already-built ISpot objects",Nothing needs to change — the real bug is inside Floor.addSpot() instead,,3,Storing a way to construct an object (a Supplier) instead of storing the object itself is what turns a lookup into an actual factory.,2

What's the simplest structural fix that would make the failure from the previous question visible instead of silent?,Add a System.exit(1) call inside release(),AvailableState.release() (and symmetrically OccupiedState.assign()) should throw an exception (e.g. IllegalStateException or a custom domain exception) instead of just printing — ParkingFacade.unPark() would then need to handle or propagate that failure instead of assuming release always succeeds,Make Ticket immutable so exitTime can never be set twice — this alone fully fixes the underlying spot-release problem too,Nothing needs to change
column2: printing to console is sufficient error handling here,,2,Throwing instead of printing turns a silent bug into a caught failure the caller must handle — immutability on Ticket alone wouldn't stop the spot's own no-op.,2

column1: What's the standard fix for the mutable-list leak found in the previous question?,Make the method synchronized,Change the field's type from List<Ticket> to Ticket[],"Return Collections.unmodifiableList(allTickets) (or a defensive copy) instead of the raw field, so callers can read but never mutate the internal state",There is no fix — Java lists are always mutable once created,,3,Wrapping the returned list (or copying it) is the standard way to expose read access without handing out write access to internal state.,1

The code comment on getAllTicketHistory() says // proxy pattern situation if this method is slow. Suppose ticket history eventually has to load from a slow database instead of an in-memory list, and you introduce a TicketHistoryProxy implements ITicketManager that wraps the real TicketManager and caches the result of the first call. Is this Proxy or Decorator?,Decorator — it wraps an object implementing the same interface and adds behavior around the wrapped call,"Neither — this would have to be Adapter, since TicketManager's own interface would need to change first",It can only be Proxy if the caching also involves a remote network call somewhere,"Proxy — even though it has the exact same wrap-and-implement-same-interface shape as Decorator, the INTENT here is controlling/optimizing access to the real object (lazy-load, cache an expensive call) rather than adding new user-facing functionality on top of it
column2: Decorator and Proxy are structurally identical, distinguished only by intent",,4,"Proxy and Decorator share identical structure — wrap plus implement the same interface — and are told apart only by why the wrapper exists, not by what it looks like in code.",3

column1: Given that Proxy and Decorator share an identical structural shape, what's the actual test for which name applies when you design a wrapper class like this?,Ask whether the wrapped object is an interface or an abstract class,"Ask whether the wrapper ADDS new behavior/responsibility the wrapped object didn't have before (Decorator, e.g. FeeDecorator adding a fee) versus CONTROLS or optimizes access to the wrapped object without changing what it conceptually does — caching, lazy init, access checks (Proxy)",Ask how many methods the wrapper class overrides,Ask whether the wrapper is constructed inside a static initializer block,,2,The distinguishing question is always about intent — adding new capability versus guarding/optimizing access to an existing one.,2

If TicketHistoryProxy only hits the real (slow) TicketManager on the FIRST call, then returns a cached copy on every later call within the same run, what has to be true about ticket history for this caching to stay safe (not return stale data)?,The cache must be invalidated (or the whole caching approach reconsidered) whenever new tickets are saved after the cache was populated — otherwise getAllTicketHistory() keeps returning an increasingly outdated snapshot even as new vehicles park
column2: a naive cache-forever Proxy is only safe if all reads happen after all writes are done,Nothing needs to be true — caching is always safe here regardless of how the underlying data changes,It only matters if TicketManager itself is implemented as a Singleton,It's safe as long as Ticket objects themselves are immutable,,1,A cache that never invalidates is only correct if nothing new is ever written after it's first populated — which isn't true for an actively running parking lot.,2

column1: Real code: List<Ticket> allTickets = new ArrayList<>(); inside TicketManager has no access modifier at all (package-private/default visibility), not private. What could another class in the SAME package (model.ticket) do that private would have prevented?,Nothing different — package-private and private behave identically in Java,It would cause a NullPointerException at runtime as soon as another class in the package is loaded,It only affects whether the field shows up in generated Javadoc,"Any other class placed in the model.ticket package could directly read AND reassign allTickets (e.g. someManager.allTickets = null
column2: ) without going through any method TicketManager provides, bypassing every guarantee its own methods try to enforce",,4,Package-private visibility opens the field to every class sharing the package — not just TicketManager's own methods.,1

column1: What's the structural fix for the SpotSize-vs-pricing coupling found in the previous question?,Merge SpotSize and vehicle type into a single enum listing every possible combination upfront,"Key PricingStrategyFactory's map by vehicle TYPE instead of by SpotSize (e.g. a Map<Class<? extends IVehicle>, IPricingStrategy>, or a distinct type identifier on IVehicle) so pricing is decided by what the vehicle actually IS, not what size spot it happens to fit into",There is no fix — pricing must always be tied to spot size in a parking lot domain,Delete PricingStrategyFactory entirely and hardcode fees directly inside Ticket,,2,"Pricing is fundamentally a vehicle-tier decision, so the lookup key should be the vehicle's own type, not the size of spot it happens to occupy.",2

Real code: Ticket stores vehicle, spot, entryTime, exitTime — no unique ticket ID field. IVehicle exposes only getSize() — no license plate/VIN. In a real gate-in/gate-out flow, what operation becomes impossible with the current model?,"A customer who has lost their physical ticket can be helped at the exit gate as long as they remember roughly when they parked, since exitTime alone is enough to identify their ticket","A customer who has lost their physical ticket cannot be helped at the exit gate — there's no ticket ID to scan or type in, and no plate number to search by
column2: the system only works if the exact same in-memory Ticket object reference is handed back, which isn't how a real physical or QR ticket system works","This only matters for TwoWheeler, not FourWheeler","It only prevents printing a receipt, nothing about actual lookup",,2,"Without any ID or vehicle-identifying field, the only way to reference a ticket again is holding onto the original object reference — unrealistic for a physical ticket workflow.",2

column1: Beyond lost-ticket lookup, what does the lack of a vehicle plate/VIN field prevent even during a completely normal (non-lost-ticket) flow?,Nothing — FourWheeler already uniquely identifies a specific car via Java's default equals(),It only affects TwoWheeler pricing calculations,"Distinguishing two different physical cars that are both FourWheeler instances — e.g. detecting that the same car is already parked and shouldn't be allowed to park again, or producing a receipt that identifies which specific vehicle was billed",It prevents SpotFinder from being able to find any spot at all,,3,"Two FourWheeler objects are indistinguishable to the system today — there's no field that ties either one to a real, specific vehicle.",1

Looking back at the whole system — Facade (ParkingFacade), Factory (SpotFactory/PricingStrategyFactory), State (AvailableState/OccupiedState), Strategy (IPricingStrategy) — which pattern decides WHAT gets built, which decides HOW an object's OWN behavior changes at runtime, and which decides WHICH interchangeable algorithm runs?,All four patterns solve the exact same problem and are interchangeable in this codebase,State decides what gets built
column2: Factory decides which algorithm runs,Strategy and State are really the same pattern under two different names,"Factory decides what gets built
column3: State decides how an object's own behavior changes at runtime (a spot switching between Available/Occupied logic)
column4: Strategy decides which interchangeable algorithm runs (which fee formula applies) — Facade doesn't decide any of these, it just hides the coordination of all three from the caller",,4,"Each pattern answers a genuinely different question — construction, internal behavior switching, and algorithm selection are three separate concerns being solved here.",2

column1: If you removed ParkingFacade entirely and had Main.java call SpotFinder, TicketManager, and PricingStrategyFactory directly (the same calls shown inside ParkingFacade's own constructor and methods today), would the underlying Factory/State/Strategy patterns still work correctly?,No — SpotFinder would stop working without ParkingFacade wrapping it,Yes — Facade is purely an organizational convenience sitting on top
column2: the other three patterns operate independently of whether a Facade wraps them or not,No — State transitions require ParkingFacade specifically to trigger them,"Yes, but only if PricingStrategyFactory is also deleted at the same time",,2,"Facade adds no behavior of its own — it only forwards to the real collaborators, so removing it doesn't change how those collaborators work.",1

column1: Quick gut-check: Main.java calls facade.parkVehicle(car) then later facade.unPark(carTicket). Inside unPark(), which single call is actually responsible for making the spot available again for the next vehicle?,ticket.getSpot().release(),ticket.setExitTime(...),strategy.calculateFee(ticket),pricingStrategyFactory.getPricingStrategy(...),,1,Everything else in unPark() is about computing and recording the fee — only getSpot().release() changes the spot's own state back to Available.,1
